To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) a considerable proportion of animal and meat isolations of phylogenetic group (phylogroup) B2 Escherichi coli are ExPEC; (ii) a substantial proportion of the virulence genes found in UTI isolates were also found in animal and meat isolats; (iii) a substantial proportion (but lower than (ii)) of antimicrobial resistance genes found in UTIs were also found in isolates from meat and animals.
the virulence and resistance genes detected in phylogroup-B2 E. coli isolations from human urinary tract infections are also present in E. coli isolats from meat and animals.

the majority of the virulence genes and antimicrobial resistance variants detected in ExPEC from UTI patients also occur in E. coli from food and food-production animals and that there is an overall similarity between E. coli from UTI patients, food, and food-production animals.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a possible zoonotic link of uropathogenic Escherichicoli (E. coli) and E. coli of animal origin.
the identification of virulence and antimicrobrial resistance genes in phylogroup 2 Escherichiacoli of human and meat origin.

a better understanding of the reservoirs of virulence genes and antimicrobial resistance in E. coli and how these reservoirs can be used to prevent the development and spread of antimicrobial resistance and virulence genes in E. coli causing human infections.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
meat and animal E. coli may be a reservoir of virulence and antimicrobials resistance genes for uropathogenic ExPEC.
meat and animals can be a source for virulence and antimicrobials resistance gene acquisition in uropathogens.
the zoonotic link is present, but that the extent is not known.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the E. coli causing the majority of UTIs in humans stem from meat and animals and that they are a reservoir of virulence and antimicrobials resistance genes.
the meat and animal E. coli isolations are not only a potential source of foodborne infections but also of UTIs.
there is a zoonotic transmission of E. coli from animals and food to humans and that these bacteria are able to adapt to their new niche.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a zoonotic connection between uropathogenic Escherichi coli (UPEC) and E. coli of meat and animal origin.
there is a zoonotic connection between E. coli from food and animals, and E. coli causing urinary tract infections.

the extended virulence and resistance profiles of the B2 isolates of animal, food and human origin were similar, and that the B2 isoltes of human origin were indistinguishable from isolates of meat and animal origin, based on the extended gene profiling.
